8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.text: Explore how Dickens uses the quotation “I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel, I am as merry as a schoolboy” to present Scrooge’s transformation.
8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.marks:

E.g. ‘Light as a feather’ suggests Scrooge’s burden of guilt has been lifted. ‘Happy as an angel’ implies spiritual joy and moral purity. ‘Merry as a schoolboy’ links to recovered innocence — the child he was in Stave 2. These directly contrast the Stave 1 similes (‘hard as flint’, ‘solitary as an oyster’), showing the completeness of his change.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment on the similes with limited analysis. E.g. These show Scrooge is now happy.

8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.text:
Read the following extract from Stave 5:

“He dressed himself ‘all in his best,’ and at last got out into the streets. The people were by this time pouring forth, as he had seen them with the Ghost of Christmas Present; and walking with his hands behind him, Scrooge regarded every one with a delighted smile. He looked so irresistibly pleasant, in a word, that three or four good-humoured fellows said, ‘Good morning, sir! A merry Christmas to you!’”

Starting with this extract, explore how Dickens presents Scrooge’s transformation and its effect on the people around him.
8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of language and structure. Contrasts with Stave 1 where ‘nobody ever stopped him in the street’ and ‘even the blind men’s dogs’ avoided him. ‘Irresistibly pleasant’ suggests his inner change is visible externally. ‘Delighted smile’ shows genuine joy, not performance. Links to Dickens’s message: when individuals change, their community responds positively. The cyclical structure means the reader measures this against Stave 1.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant textual contrast.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments with some comparison to Stave 1.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments about Scrooge being happy.

8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.text:
Read the following extract from the end of Stave 5:

“Scrooge was better than his word. He did it all, and infinitely more; and to Tiny Tim, who did NOT die, he was a second father. He became as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man, as the good old city knew.”

Starting with this extract, explore how Dickens presents the theme of redemption in A Christmas Carol.
8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of language, structure, and context. Explores the repetition of ‘good’ (five times) as emphasising completeness of change. ‘Better than his word’ means actions exceeded promises. ‘Second father’ to Tiny Tim shows Scrooge accepting social responsibility — the key message of the novella. ‘Did NOT die’ (Dickens’s emphasis) is the emotional reward for both Scrooge and the reader. Links to Victorian context: Dickens arguing that wealthy people can save lives through generosity.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant references and some context.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments with some language analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments about redemption.

8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.text: How does Dickens use the cyclical structure of A Christmas Carol to reinforce his message about the possibility of change?
8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.marks:
Top band (10-12): Convincing analysis exploring how Stave 5 mirrors Stave 1 in setting (weather), characters (carol singer, charity collector, Fred, Bob), and tone. Discusses how the cyclical structure allows the reader to measure transformation precisely. Analyses specific contrasts: ‘cold, bleak, biting’ becomes ‘Golden sunlight; Heavenly sky’; rejection of charity becomes generous donation; cruelty to Bob becomes ‘I’ll raise your salary.’ Links to Dickens’s purpose: the structure is optimistic — wrongs can be put right, people can change.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear analysis with relevant structural comparisons.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Supported comments with some structural awareness.
Lower band (1-3): Simple statements about the beginning and ending.

8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.text:
Starting with the following extract from Stave 5, explore how Dickens presents the importance of generosity and social responsibility in A Christmas Carol.

“‘My dear sir,’ said Scrooge, quickening his pace, and taking the old gentleman by both his hands. ‘How do you do? I hope you succeeded yesterday. It was very kind of you. A merry Christmas to you, sir!’”

Write about:
• how Dickens presents generosity in this extract
• how Dickens presents generosity and social responsibility in the novella as a whole.
[30 marks]
8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.marks:

Analyses ‘quickening his pace’ as urgency to do good — contrasting his former reluctance. ‘Both his hands’ shows warmth and physical connection vs Stave 1 isolation. ‘Back-payments’ implies acknowledgement of years of neglect. Explores generosity across the novella: Fezziwig’s party (costs little, gives much), the Cratchits (generous in spirit despite poverty), Fred (offers love despite rejection). Links to Dickens’s social purpose: the novella as a call to wealthy Victorians to take responsibility for poverty. References Malthus, the Poor Law, and Dickens’s own experience of poverty.

Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of how thought and action become simultaneous. Contrasts with Macbeth’s earlier agonised soliloquies. Explores how the removal of moral reflection signals complete corruption.
Lower band (1-2): Basic understanding of impulsive action.

5fffe156-802c-449e-9950-02c8ea9d10d1.text: Read the extract from Act 4, Scene 2 (the murder of Lady Macduff and her son). How does Shakespeare create pathos and horror in this extract?
5fffe156-802c-449e-9950-02c8ea9d10d1.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of the child’s bravery, the domestic setting, and the contrast between innocence and violence. Explores how Shakespeare ensures the audience turns against Macbeth.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple awareness.

6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.text: Explore how Dickens uses the quotation “Mankind was my business” to present Marley’s role in the novella and Dickens’s wider message.
6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis linking the quotation to Dickens’s message. E.g. ‘Mankind’ is emphatic — Marley now realises that helping others should have been his life’s purpose. ‘Business’ has a double meaning: Marley focused on financial business, but his real business should have been caring for people. The italicised emphasis (in the original text) shows Marley’s anguish. Dickens uses Marley as a mouthpiece for his own social message.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment with limited analysis. E.g. This shows Marley wishes he had been kinder.

6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.text:
Read the following extract from Stave 1:

“Oh! But he was a tight-fisted hand at the grindstone, Scrooge! a squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous, old sinner! Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire, secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster.”

Starting with this extract, explore how Dickens presents Scrooge as an isolated and selfish character.
6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of language and structure. Explores the list of aggressive present participles (‘squeezing, wrenching, grasping’) as creating relentless energy of greed. ‘Hard and sharp as flint’ = cold, dangerous, incapable of warmth (‘no steel had ever struck out generous fire’). ‘Solitary as an oyster’ = sealed shut, refusing to open up. Links to Dickens’s purpose: establishing Scrooge at his worst so that his transformation is more dramatic. Contrasts with Stave 5 similes.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant language exploration.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments with some reference to techniques.
Lower band (1-2): Simple description of Scrooge as mean.

6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.text:
Read the following extract from Stave 3 about the Cratchit family Christmas:

“Bob held his withered little hand in his, as if he loved the child, and wished to keep him by his side, and dreaded that he might be taken from him.”

Starting with this extract, explore how Dickens uses the Cratchit family to present the struggles of the poor.
6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. Explores ‘withered little hand’ as suggesting premature decay — a child’s hand should not be withered. The tricolon (‘loved’, ‘wished’, ‘dreaded’) shows escalating emotion from love to fear. ‘Taken from him’ implies death, yet Bob cannot prevent it because of poverty. Links to Stave 4 where Tim dies, fulfilling this fear. Discusses Dickens’s message: wealthy people like Scrooge have the power to prevent such suffering.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant language and structural links.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments with some analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification of Bob’s love for Tim.

6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.text: How does Dickens use the character of Fred to present the true meaning of Christmas and to challenge Scrooge’s attitudes?
6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.marks:
Top band (10-12): Convincing analysis. Explores Fred as the embodiment of Christmas spirit: ‘a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time.’ Analyses Fred as a foil to Scrooge — same family, opposite values. Fred’s persistence in inviting Scrooge despite rejection models Dickens’s message about never giving up on people. Links Fred to Fan and the theme of family. Discusses Fred’s role in Stave 5 when Scrooge finally accepts the invitation, completing the reconciliation. References Dickens’s context: Christmas as a time for social unity.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear analysis with relevant references.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Supported comments with some analysis.
Lower band (1-3): Simple statements about Fred being kind.

6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.text:
Starting with the following extract, explore how Dickens presents the theme of social responsibility through the character of Scrooge in A Christmas Carol.

“‘Are there no prisons?’ asked Scrooge.
‘Plenty of prisons,’ said the gentleman.
‘And the Union workhouses?’ demanded Scrooge. ‘Are they still in operation?’”

Write about:
• how Dickens presents Scrooge’s attitudes in this extract
• how Dickens challenges these attitudes in the novella as a whole.
[30 marks]
6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.marks:
Top band (26-30) Convincing, critical response. Analyses Scrooge’s questions as rhetorical — he already knows the answer and is dismissing the charity collector. ‘Demanded’ shows aggression. References to prisons and workhouses echo real Victorian institutions. Links to Malthus (‘surplus population’). Traces how Dickens systematically challenges these attitudes: Marley’s chain (consequences of neglect), Fezziwig (alternative model of wealth), Cratchits (human cost of poverty), Ignorance and Want (Scrooge’s own words thrown back at him), the grave (final reckoning). Argues Dickens wrote the novella as a direct challenge to wealthy Victorians who shared Scrooge’s attitudes.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful response with clear analysis and context.
Top band (16-20): Clear understanding with explained comments.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained comments with references.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments with some textual reference.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments with limited reference.

6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.text: Explore how Dickens uses contrast between Fezziwig and Scrooge to present his message about the responsibilities of employers.
6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.marks:
Top band (10-12): Convincing analysis. Contrasts Fezziwig’s joyful, generous personality (‘laughed all over himself’) with Scrooge’s cold, aggressive introduction (‘squeezing, wrenching, grasping’). Explores Scrooge’s own recognition: ‘The happiness he gives, is quite as great as if it cost a fortune’ — showing that kindness costs nothing but means everything. Links to the Victorian context: factory owners who exploited workers. Discusses how Fezziwig makes Scrooge reflect on his treatment of Bob Cratchit.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear analysis with relevant contrasts.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Supported comments with some textual reference.
Lower band (1-3): Simple statements about the two employers.

a57c134a-be5a-450a-a2f2-b3b4782a64d0.text: Analyse how Dickens uses the word ‘humbug’ to reveal Scrooge’s attitude towards Christmas in Stave 1.
a57c134a-be5a-450a-a2f2-b3b4782a64d0.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis showing ‘humbug’ means fraud/nonsense, revealing Scrooge sees Christmas as worthless. Links to Dickens’s purpose — Scrooge represents wealthy Victorians who dismissed generosity. Explores effect on the reader: immediate dislike of Scrooge.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that ‘humbug’ shows Scrooge dislikes Christmas, with little analysis of why Dickens uses it.

a57c134a-be5a-450a-a2f2-b3b4782a64d0.text:
Read the following extract from Stave 1:

‘Are there no prisons?’ asked Scrooge. ‘And the Union workhouses?’

Starting with this extract, how does Dickens present Scrooge’s attitude towards the poor?
a57c134a-be5a-450a-a2f2-b3b4782a64d0.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. Scrooge’s rhetorical questions show he believes prisons and workhouses are sufficient help for the poor — he sees no need for charity. Links to Malthusian attitudes and the Poor Law. Explores Dickens’s purpose: Scrooge represents the callous upper classes. Analyses effect of the questions on the reader — creates disgust.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with some context, e.g. links to Victorian attitudes or Dickens’s purpose.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid points about Scrooge’s attitude with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments about Scrooge being mean.

a57c134a-be5a-450a-a2f2-b3b4782a64d0.text:
Read the following extract:

‘If they would rather die,’ said Scrooge, ‘they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population.’

How does Dickens use Scrooge’s language here to criticise Victorian attitudes towards poverty?
a57c134a-be5a-450a-a2f2-b3b4782a64d0.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive response linking ‘surplus population’ to Malthusian economics. Analyses how ‘decrease’ dehumanises the poor, reducing them to statistics. Explores Dickens’s purpose: using Scrooge as a vehicle to expose and condemn real Victorian attitudes. Notes that these words are echoed by the Ghost of Christmas Present in Stave 3, showing their cruelty.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis linking language to context, with some exploration of purpose.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid comments on Scrooge’s cruelty with limited context.
Lower band (1-2): Simple statement that Scrooge is cruel.

a57c134a-be5a-450a-a2f2-b3b4782a64d0.text: How does Dickens use A Christmas Carol as a whole to challenge Victorian attitudes towards poverty and social responsibility?
a57c134a-be5a-450a-a2f2-b3b4782a64d0.marks:
Top band (10-12): Convincing, critical response. Explores multiple methods: Scrooge as representative of the wealthy; the Cratchits as sympathetic victims of poverty; Ignorance and Want as allegorical warnings; Marley’s chain as symbol of moral failure. Links to Malthus, the Poor Law, and Dickens’s personal experience. Analyses how the redemption arc suggests change is possible.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear, explained response with relevant references and some analysis of methods and context.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Supported response with some relevant points but limited analysis.
Lower band (1-3): Simple, limited comments about the text.

a57c134a-be5a-450a-a2f2-b3b4782a64d0.text:
Starting with the opening of Stave 1, explore how Dickens presents Scrooge as a product of Victorian society.

Write about:
• how Dickens presents Scrooge in Stave 1
• how Dickens uses the whole novella to explore why people like Scrooge exist and how they can change.

[30 marks]
a57c134a-be5a-450a-a2f2-b3b4782a64d0.marks:
AO1 (12 marks): Critical, exploratory response using textual references. Must cover both bullet points with well-chosen quotations.

AO2 (12 marks): Analyses Dickens’s methods — e.g. the list of adjectives (‘squeezing, wrenching, grasping’), cold/weather imagery, Malthusian language, the structural contrast between Staves 1 and 5. Explores effects on the reader.

AO3 (6 marks): Shows understanding of Victorian context — the Poor Law, workhouses, Malthusian economics, child labour, the Industrial Revolution, Dickens’s biography. Links context to Dickens’s purpose throughout.

Top-band responses will argue that Scrooge is both a product of and a challenge to Victorian society, using the redemption arc to show that individual change is possible.

a57c134a-be5a-450a-a2f2-b3b4782a64d0.text: Explain why Dickens chose to write a novella rather than a political pamphlet to communicate his views on poverty.
a57c134a-be5a-450a-a2f2-b3b4782a64d0.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed explanation. A story could reach people’s emotions in a way that facts and statistics could not. Dickens used characters like Scrooge and Tiny Tim to create empathy. The Gothic/ghost story elements made it entertaining and memorable. Christmas setting meant readers were already thinking about generosity. References Dickens’s walk through Manchester as the moment he chose fiction over non-fiction.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment that a story is more interesting than an essay.

a98b0878-6443-462f-bb6d-79de1856bd42.text: Starting with Act 1, Scene 3, explore how Shakespeare presents Macbeth’s ambition as a destructive force.
a98b0878-6443-462f-bb6d-79de1856bd42.marks:
Top band (30-34) Convincing, critical exploration of ambition as hamartia. Perceptive analysis of Shakespeare’s methods (soliloquy, metaphor, dramatic irony). Well-integrated context about tragic conventions and Jacobean values. Precise terminology. Excellent spelling/grammar.
Upper band (25-29) Thoughtful analysis with clear understanding of Shakespeare’s craft.
Upper-mid band (19-24): Clear understanding with some analysis of methods.
Mid band (13-18): Explained response with some relevant comments.
Lower-mid band (7-12): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-6): Simple comments.

a98b0878-6443-462f-bb6d-79de1856bd42.text: How does Shakespeare use the metaphor of “vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself” to convey Macbeth’s understanding of his own flaw?
a98b0878-6443-462f-bb6d-79de1856bd42.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of the equestrian metaphor. Explains how “o’erleaps” suggests ambition that overreaches and self-destructs. Links to the concept of hamartia and tragic structure.
Lower band (1-2): Basic understanding of the quote’s meaning.

a98b0878-6443-462f-bb6d-79de1856bd42.text: Read the extract from Act 1, Scene 3 where Macbeth first hears the prophecies. How does Shakespeare present Macbeth’s inner conflict in this extract?
a98b0878-6443-462f-bb6d-79de1856bd42.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of Macbeth’s aside and soliloquy. Explores the contrast between public composure and private turmoil. Notes “horrible imaginings” and the significance of “murder” entering his thoughts unprompted.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant textual support.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some supported comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple awareness of conflict.

a98b0878-6443-462f-bb6d-79de1856bd42.text: Explain how Shakespeare uses Banquo as a foil to Macbeth. Refer to their different responses to the witches’ prophecies.
a98b0878-6443-462f-bb6d-79de1856bd42.marks:
Top band (25-30): Convincing comparison of both characters’ responses. Explores Banquo’s caution (“instruments of darkness”) versus Macbeth’s immediate scheming. Links to Shakespeare’s purpose: showing that Macbeth’s fall is a choice, not fate.
Upper-mid band (18-24): Clear comparison with relevant evidence.
Lower-mid band (10-17): Some comparison with limited evidence.
Lower band (1-9): Simple comments.

a98b0878-6443-462f-bb6d-79de1856bd42.text: How does Shakespeare’s presentation of Macbeth in Act 1, Scene 2 create dramatic irony once we learn of his ambition?
a98b0878-6443-462f-bb6d-79de1856bd42.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of the Captain’s report (“brave Macbeth,” “unseamed him”). Explores how Shakespeare establishes Macbeth as a loyal hero, making his later betrayal more shocking. Notes the irony of receiving a traitor’s title.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis of dramatic irony.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

a98b0878-6443-462f-bb6d-79de1856bd42.text: Analyse how Shakespeare uses the line “Stars, hide your fires” to reveal Macbeth’s moral awareness.
a98b0878-6443-462f-bb6d-79de1856bd42.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of the imperative and light/dark imagery. Explains that Macbeth wants to hide his desires from heaven, showing he knows they are sinful. Links to Jacobean beliefs about divine judgement.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment on the quotation.

8e4515d4-cb7e-48a2-98f3-1cdfe077f8bd.text: Analyse how Dickens uses the simile ‘solitary as an oyster’ to present Scrooge’s character in Stave 1.
8e4515d4-cb7e-48a2-98f3-1cdfe077f8bd.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis. An oyster is sealed shut, hard-shelled, and hides itself away — Scrooge is emotionally closed off, refusing connection with others. Oysters also contain pearls, which could suggest hidden potential for good beneath Scrooge’s hard exterior. Links to Dickens’s wider purpose: even the most closed-off people can change.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment that Scrooge is lonely, with limited analysis of the image.

8e4515d4-cb7e-48a2-98f3-1cdfe077f8bd.text:
Read the following extract from Stave 1, where Fred visits Scrooge:

‘Christmas a humbug, uncle!’ said Scrooge’s nephew. ‘You don’t mean that, I am sure?’ ‘I do,’ said Scrooge. ‘Merry Christmas! What right have you to be merry? What reason have you to be merry? You’re poor enough.’

Starting with this extract, how does Dickens use the relationship between Scrooge and Fred to present different attitudes to Christmas?
8e4515d4-cb7e-48a2-98f3-1cdfe077f8bd.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. Scrooge equates happiness with wealth (‘you’re poor enough’) while Fred equates it with generosity and goodwill. Fred as foil and author surrogate. Analyses rhetorical questions showing Scrooge’s aggression. Explores wider novella: Fred’s persistence pays off in Stave 5 when Scrooge joins his Christmas dinner.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with some context or wider references.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid points about the contrast with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments about Scrooge being grumpy.

8e4515d4-cb7e-48a2-98f3-1cdfe077f8bd.text:
Read the following extract from Stave 1:

‘I wear the chain I forged in life,’ replied the Ghost. ‘I made it link by link, and yard by yard.’

Starting with this extract, how does Dickens use Marley’s ghost to present ideas about guilt and consequences?
8e4515d4-cb7e-48a2-98f3-1cdfe077f8bd.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive response. The chain as symbol of accumulated greed — built gradually through selfish choices. Analyses repetition (‘link by link, yard by yard’) showing deliberate, incremental moral failure. Marley as warning figure. ‘Mankind was my business’ as Dickens’s central message. Links to wider novella: Scrooge’s chain is even longer, raising the stakes.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis of symbolism with some wider references.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some understanding of the chain as symbol with limited development.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comment that Marley has a chain because he was bad.

8e4515d4-cb7e-48a2-98f3-1cdfe077f8bd.text: How does Dickens use Stave 1 to establish the themes that will drive Scrooge’s transformation throughout the rest of the novella?
8e4515d4-cb7e-48a2-98f3-1cdfe077f8bd.marks:
Top band (10-12): Convincing, critical response exploring multiple themes: isolation (oyster simile, darkness imagery), greed (Marley’s chain, charity collectors scene), social responsibility (‘Mankind was my business’), and the possibility of redemption (Marley’s warning, three spirits). Analyses methods: Gothic atmosphere, foils, symbolism, foreshadowing. Links to Dickens’s purpose.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear response covering at least two themes with relevant references.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some relevant points with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-3): Simple comments.

8e4515d4-cb7e-48a2-98f3-1cdfe077f8bd.text:
Starting with the description of Scrooge at the beginning of Stave 1, explore how Dickens presents the effects of greed on a person’s character and relationships.

Write about:
• how Dickens presents the effects of greed in Stave 1
• how Dickens presents the effects of greed in the novella as a whole.

[30 marks]
8e4515d4-cb7e-48a2-98f3-1cdfe077f8bd.marks:
AO1 (12 marks): Critical, exploratory response with well-chosen textual references covering both bullet points. Must discuss Stave 1 in detail and range across the novella.

AO2 (12 marks): Analyses Dickens’s methods — the list of adjectives (‘squeezing, wrenching, grasping’), similes (‘solitary as an oyster’, ‘hard and sharp as flint’), Marley’s chain symbolism, pathetic fallacy, contrast with Fred/Bob. In the wider novella: Fezziwig as contrast, Belle’s rejection, Scrooge’s lonely death in Stave 4, transformation in Stave 5.

AO3 (6 marks): Victorian context — Malthusian attitudes, the Poor Law, Dickens’s personal experience of poverty, the role of wealthy industrialists. Links context to purpose throughout.

Top-band responses will track how greed distorts every aspect of Scrooge’s life and argue that Dickens uses the novella to show greed as both a personal failing and a societal disease.

8e4515d4-cb7e-48a2-98f3-1cdfe077f8bd.text: Analyse how Dickens uses the phrase ‘Darkness is cheap, and Scrooge liked it’ to reveal Scrooge’s values.
8e4515d4-cb7e-48a2-98f3-1cdfe077f8bd.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis. ‘Cheap’ links to Scrooge’s obsession with saving money — even his choice of darkness is an economic decision. ‘Darkness’ symbolises moral blindness and spiritual emptiness. The fact that Scrooge ‘liked it’ suggests he actively chooses ignorance and isolation. Links to wider motif of light vs darkness across the novella (the Ghost of Christmas Past’s light, the Ghost of Christmas Present’s torch).
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment that Scrooge is mean and likes saving money.

078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.text: Explore how Dickens uses the quotation “I fear you more than any spectre I have seen” to present Scrooge’s response to the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come.
078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of language choices with clear effect. E.g. The word ‘spectre’ has Gothic connotations of death and the supernatural. ‘More than any’ shows escalation — each ghost has intensified Scrooge’s emotional response. The admission of fear shows Scrooge is now emotionally vulnerable, contrasting his dismissiveness in Stave 1.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment on the quotation with limited analysis. E.g. This shows Scrooge is scared of the ghost.

078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.text:
Read the following extract from Stave 4:

“A churchyard. Here, then; the wretched man whose name he had now to learn, lay underneath the ground. It was a worthy place. Walled in by houses; overrun by grass and weeds, the growth of vegetation’s death, not life; choked up with too much burying; fat with repleted appetite. A worthy place!”

Starting with this extract, explore how Dickens uses setting to convey ideas about death and moral failure.
078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of language, structure, and context. Explores ‘vegetation’s death, not life’ as an oxymoron reflecting spiritual emptiness. ‘Choked up’ and ‘fat with repleted appetite’ personify the graveyard as overfed on death — mirroring how Scrooge has consumed wealth without giving back. The ironic repetition of ‘worthy place’ highlights how Scrooge’s life has led to a worthless end. Links to Victorian context: neglected graves for the unmourned.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with some language exploration and contextual links.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments on the extract with some relevant points.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments with limited textual reference.

078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.text:
Read the following extract from Stave 4:

“The ways were foul and narrow; the shops and houses wretched; the people half-naked, drunken, slipshod, ugly.”

Starting with this extract, explore how Dickens presents the effects of poverty in A Christmas Carol.
078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis connecting extract to wider novel. Explores the list of adjectives ‘foul’, ‘wretched’, ‘drunken’ as creating a catalogue of degradation. Links to Ignorance and Want from Stave 3 — these are the consequences Dickens warned about. Discusses how Old Joe’s customers are driven to crime by want, not inherent wickedness. References Dickens’s social purpose: making Victorian readers confront poverty they preferred to ignore.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with some language features and links to the wider text.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments with some relevant references.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification of poverty with minimal analysis.

078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.text: How does Dickens use the juxtaposition of Scrooge’s death and Tiny Tim’s death in Stave 4 to present his message about social responsibility?
078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.marks:
Top band (10-12): Convincing, critical analysis. Explores how Scrooge dies alone, robbed, and unmourned while Tiny Tim is mourned with genuine love and tenderness. Analyses specific language: businessmen’s indifference vs Bob’s grief. Links to Dickens’s message: wealth without compassion leads to spiritual death; generosity even in poverty creates meaning. References Victorian context — Malthusian attitudes, the Poor Law, Dickens’s social reform agenda. Discusses structural purpose: juxtaposition as the final push toward Scrooge’s transformation.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear, explained analysis with relevant textual references and some contextual links.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Supported comments with some analysis of language or structure.
Lower band (1-3): Simple statements about the two deaths with limited analysis.

078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.text:
Starting with the extract below, explore how Dickens presents fear and its power to change people in A Christmas Carol.

“Scrooge crept towards it, trembling as he went; and following the finger, read upon the stone of the neglected grave his own name, Ebenezer Scrooge. ‘Am I that man who lay upon the bed?’ he cried, upon his knees.”

Write about:
• how Dickens presents fear in this extract
• how Dickens presents fear and its effects in the novella as a whole.
[30 marks]
078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.marks:
Top band (26-30) Convincing, critical, exploratory response. Analyses ‘crept’ and ‘trembling’ as showing Scrooge’s physical terror. Explores ‘neglected grave’ as reflecting his neglected moral life. Discusses the progression of fear across staves: unease (Marley), discomfort (Past), guilt (Present), terror (Yet to Come). Links to Gothic conventions and Dickens’s moral purpose. Argues fear is redemptive — without it, Scrooge could not change. References Victorian context: the novella as a warning to wealthy readers.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful, developed response with clear analysis and contextual understanding.
Top band (16-20): Clear understanding with explained comments and relevant references.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained comments with appropriate references.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments with some relevant textual reference.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments with limited reference to the text.

078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.text: Explore how Dickens uses the silence of the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come to create tension and convey his message about the consequences of a selfish life.
078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.marks:
Top band (10-12): Convincing analysis exploring the ghost’s silence as more terrifying than speech. Discusses the pointing finger as the only communication — forcing Scrooge to draw his own conclusions. Contrasts with previous ghosts: Past speaks gently, Present speaks warmly, Yet to Come says nothing. Explores the Gothic tradition of the silent death figure. Links silence to Dickens’s message: the future offers no comfort or explanation — only consequences.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear analysis with relevant textual references.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Supported comments with some analysis.

4801952c-0f06-4ac9-8671-84a261ebb718.text: Analyse how Dickens uses the phrase ‘overcome with penitence and grief’ to show the change in Scrooge during Stave 3.
4801952c-0f06-4ac9-8671-84a261ebb718.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis. ‘Penitence’ has religious connotations — Scrooge is not just sorry but seeking moral forgiveness, connecting to the theme of redemption. ‘Grief’ suggests genuine sorrow, not performance. ‘Overcome’ implies he cannot control his emotions — a stark contrast to the self-contained Scrooge of Stave 1. Links to Dickens’s structural purpose: each stave deepens Scrooge’s emotional response.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment that Scrooge feels sorry.

4801952c-0f06-4ac9-8671-84a261ebb718.text:
Read the following extract from Stave 3:

‘No one said or thought it was a small pudding for a large family. It would have been flat heresy to do so. Any Cratchit would have blushed to hint at such a thing.’

Starting with this extract, how does Dickens present the Cratchit family’s attitude to their poverty?
4801952c-0f06-4ac9-8671-84a261ebb718.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. ‘Flat heresy’ is a religious term — complaining about the pudding would be like blasphemy, suggesting the Cratchits treat gratitude as sacred. ‘Blushed’ shows their embarrassment at the idea of ingratitude. Explores Dickens’s purpose: the Cratchits’ dignity in poverty shames Scrooge’s wealth without happiness. Wider references to ‘eked out’, ‘twice-turned gown’, and the ‘family display of glass’.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with some wider references.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid points about the family being grateful.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comment that the family is happy.

4801952c-0f06-4ac9-8671-84a261ebb718.text:
Read the following extract from Stave 3:

‘Yellow, meagre, ragged, scowling, wolfish; but prostrate, too, in their humility.’

Starting with this extract, how does Dickens present the suffering of the poor through the figures of Ignorance and Want?
4801952c-0f06-4ac9-8671-84a261ebb718.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive response. The list of adjectives creates an overwhelming picture of deprivation. ‘Wolfish’ dehumanises the children — poverty has made them animal-like. ‘Prostrate in their humility’ suggests they are beaten down by society yet still submissive. Analyses the allegorical meaning: Ignorance (society’s blindness) and Want (deprivation). Links the Ghost’s warning (‘Doom’) to Dickens’s political message about the consequences of ignoring poverty.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with some reference to allegory or context.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some understanding of the children’s appearance with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple description of the children.

4801952c-0f06-4ac9-8671-84a261ebb718.text: How does Dickens use Stave 3 to develop his argument that the wealthy have a moral responsibility to help the poor?
4801952c-0f06-4ac9-8671-84a261ebb718.marks:
Top band (10-12): Convincing, critical response. Explores multiple methods: the Cratchits’ dignity shaming Scrooge’s excess; Tiny Tim as emotional catalyst; the Ghost echoing Scrooge’s words to expose their cruelty; Ignorance and Want as allegorical warning. Analyses the symbolism of the Ghost (abundance, peace) as representing what society should aspire to. Links to Malthus, the Poor Law, and Dickens’s context.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear response with relevant references and some analysis of methods.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Supported response with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-3): Simple comments.

4801952c-0f06-4ac9-8671-84a261ebb718.text:
Starting with the Cratchit family’s Christmas dinner in Stave 3, explore how Dickens presents the suffering of the poor in A Christmas Carol.

Write about:
• how Dickens presents the suffering of the poor in this extract
• how Dickens presents the suffering of the poor in the novella as a whole.

[30 marks]
4801952c-0f06-4ac9-8671-84a261ebb718.marks:
AO1 (12 marks): Critical, exploratory response. Must cover both bullet points: detailed analysis of the Cratchit dinner scene (cheapness, eked out, twice-turned gown, Tiny Tim), and wider novella references (Ignorance and Want, Stave 4 future, the charity collectors in Stave 1, Marley’s chain).

AO2 (12 marks): Analyses methods — the ironic ‘display of glass’, pathetic fallacy, the list of adjectives for Ignorance and Want, the Ghost echoing Scrooge’s words, Tiny Tim’s ‘withered little hand’. Explores structural devices: placing the Cratchits’ warmth alongside Ignorance and Want creates emotional whiplash.

AO3 (6 marks): Victorian context — the working poor, child mortality, disability without healthcare, Malthusian attitudes, the Poor Law. Dickens’s personal experience of poverty. Links to purpose throughout.

Top-band responses will argue that Dickens uses a range of methods to present poverty not as a statistic but as a human experience, making it impossible for the reader to remain indifferent.

4801952c-0f06-4ac9-8671-84a261ebb718.text: Analyse how Dickens uses the Ghost of Christmas Present’s empty scabbard to symbolise the meaning of Christmas.
4801952c-0f06-4ac9-8671-84a261ebb718.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis. The scabbard once held a sword, but the sword is gone and the sheath is ‘eaten up with rust’ — suggesting weapons have not been needed for a long time. Christmas is presented as a time of peace, not conflict. The rust implies this peace is ancient, linking Christmas to centuries of tradition. Connects to the Ghost’s bare breast and open hand, which also symbolise vulnerability and generosity.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment that the scabbard is empty, meaning there is no fighting.

057ffc65-3d81-4020-9efc-bca1190d2cc5.text: Starting with the banquet scene (Act 3, Scene 4), explore how Shakespeare uses the ghost of Banquo to present Macbeth’s guilt.

057ffc65-3d81-4020-9efc-bca1190d2cc5.text: How does Shakespeare use the image of the “fruitless crown” and “barren sceptre” to convey Macbeth’s despair?

057ffc65-3d81-4020-9efc-bca1190d2cc5.text: Read the extract from Act 3, Scene 4 where Macbeth sees Banquo’s ghost. How does Shakespeare create dramatic tension in this extract?

057ffc65-3d81-4020-9efc-bca1190d2cc5.text: Explain how Shakespeare presents Macbeth’s transformation from reluctant murderer to calculating tyrant across Acts 1 to 3.

057ffc65-3d81-4020-9efc-bca1190d2cc5.text: How does Shakespeare use the metaphor “I am in blood / Stepped in so far” to convey Macbeth’s moral position?

057ffc65-3d81-4020-9efc-bca1190d2cc5.text: Read the extract from Act 3, Scene 1 where Macbeth reflects on Banquo. How does Shakespeare present Macbeth’s fear and jealousy in this extract?

bcfb5434-c373-46b0-923c-9265647eb679.text: How does Shakespeare use the phrase “Out, damned spot!” to show the effects of guilt on Lady Macbeth?

bcfb5434-c373-46b0-923c-9265647eb679.text: Read the extract from Act 5, Scene 1 (the sleepwalking scene). How does Shakespeare present Lady Macbeth’s mental collapse in this extract?

bcfb5434-c373-46b0-923c-9265647eb679.text: Explain how Shakespeare uses Lady Macbeth’s character arc to explore the consequences of defying natural order. Trace her journey from Act 1 to Act 5.

bcfb5434-c373-46b0-923c-9265647eb679.text: How does the Doctor’s line “More needs she the divine than the physician” connect to the play’s wider themes?

e063d513-1e5b-48ef-8956-ccdf995a1d3d.text: How does Dickens present the theme of redemption in A Christmas Carol?

e063d513-1e5b-48ef-8956-ccdf995a1d3d.text: How does Dickens use the character of Scrooge to present his views about wealth and society?

e063d513-1e5b-48ef-8956-ccdf995a1d3d.text: What is the significance of the three Christmas spirits in the novella's moral message?
